271.event_title: Margaret Fox confesses that the spirit rappings were a hoax
271.place: Academy of Music, New York City, United States
271.event: In 1848 the young sisters Margaret and Kate Fox of Hydesville, New York, began producing rapping sounds that they presented as messages from spirits, and their seances helped launch the Spiritualist movement. In October 1888 Margaret told the New York World, and then a public audience at the New York Academy of Music, that the raps had been a fraud produced chiefly by movements of the joints of their toes. She retracted the confession the following year.
271.explanation: Four decades of claimed contact with the spirit world turned out to have come from the sisters' own bodies.
271.tie_back: The kural says the five elements of the hypocrite's own body laugh at his false show of holiness, and in the Fox case the deceivers' own bodies were the secret source of the sham.
271._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of sham spirituality betrayed from within the body, though the Fox sisters were mediums rather than ascetics.

272.event_title: Rousseau, author of a famous book on education, gives up his own children
272.event: By his own account, Jean-Jacques Rousseau and his partner Therese Levasseur had five children, and each was left at the Paris foundling hospital shortly after birth. In 1762 Rousseau published Emile, or On Education, which became one of the most influential works ever written on bringing up children. His abandonment of his children was later used against him by Voltaire, and in his Confessions Rousseau acknowledged and tried to justify what he had done.
272.explanation: The gap between Rousseau's celebrated public teaching and his private conduct became one of the best-known examples of a moral authority undercut by what he knew of himself.
272.tie_back: The kural asks what use a sky-high appearance of virtue is when the heart knows its own faults, and Rousseau's own Confessions record the fault behind his lofty reputation.
272._accuracy_note: A reasonable to strong fit for the gap between lofty reputation and self-known fault, though Rousseau's public image was that of a moral thinker rather than a holy man.

273.place: Kopenick, near Berlin, German Empire (now Germany)
273.event: Wilhelm Voigt, an unemployed shoemaker with a criminal record, put together a Prussian army captain's uniform from second-hand pieces. Wearing it, he ordered a squad of about ten real soldiers to follow him to the town hall of Kopenick, where they arrested the mayor and the treasurer on his orders and he took about 4,000 marks from the town treasury. He was arrested ten days later and sentenced to four years in prison.
273.explanation: The episode became a byword for how a borrowed uniform could make soldiers and officials obey a man with no real authority at all.
273.tie_back: The kural compares the weak man in the imposing garb of an ascetic to a cow grazing on crops in a tiger's skin, and Voigt fed himself from the town's treasury by wearing a captain's borrowed form.
273._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the tiger-skin image, though the borrowed garb was military rather than religious.

274.event_title: Ferdinand Waldo Demara serves as a naval surgeon under a false name
274.place: HMCS Cayuga, off the coast of Korea
274.event: Ferdinand Waldo Demara, an American who had earlier passed himself off in several religious orders, took the identity of a real doctor, Joseph Cyr, whom he had met while living with a religious order in Maine. In March 1951 he offered his services to the Royal Canadian Navy as Dr Cyr, was commissioned as a surgeon-lieutenant without his credentials being checked, and served aboard the destroyer HMCS Cayuga in Korean waters, where he treated wounded men. He was exposed as an impostor some months later.
274.explanation: Demara repeatedly hid behind trusted roles, from monk to doctor, which led people to accept him without question.
274.tie_back: The kural likens the man who hides behind a sacred garb to a hunter hidden in a bush, and Demara used respected roles as cover in just that way.
274._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Demara hid behind trusted roles, including religious ones, but the documented harm to those he deceived is limited and the kural's predatory image is only partly matched.

275.place: Hampton Court, London and Leicester, England
275.event: Thomas Wolsey, a cardinal of the Church and Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor, accumulated enormous wealth, with an income at its peak estimated at many times that of the richest nobleman, and built Hampton Court Palace. When he failed to obtain the pope's annulment of Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, he fell from favour in 1529 and was stripped of his offices except the archbishopric of York. In November 1530 he was arrested on a charge of treason and died at Leicester Abbey on his way south to face it.
275.explanation: A churchman vowed to spiritual service who had amassed worldly power and riches lost all of it within a single year.
275.tie_back: The kural warns that those who claim to have renounced attachment while clinging to the world will meet many sorrows, and Wolsey's sudden ruin fits that warning.
275._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for a churchman's worldly attachment ending in sorrow, though Wolsey never pretended to be an ascetic and his fall was caused by politics rather than exposure of hypocrisy.

276.event: Moliere's comedy Tartuffe, about a man who feigns intense piety in order to gain control of a trusting family's household and fortune, was first performed before Louis XIV at Versailles on 12 May 1664. After attacks from devout critics, the king banned public performances, and a revised version was banned again in Paris in 1667. Public performance was finally permitted on 5 February 1669, and the play became one of the most successful in the French repertoire.
276.explanation: Tartuffe's name became a byword in French and English for the religious hypocrite who preys on the trust of the devout.
276.tie_back: The kural says none are more hard-hearted than those who live by deceiving others while posing as renunciants, which is precisely the character Moliere put on the stage.
276._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the kural's type, though the hypocrite himself is fictional and the real event is the controversy over the play.

277.event_title: The collapse of Ivar Kreuger, the Match King
277.event: The Swedish financier Ivar Kreuger built a business empire that controlled much of the world's match production and lent large sums to governments, and he was widely admired as a financial genius. After his death in Paris in March 1932, auditors from Price Waterhouse found that many of the assets and profits recorded by his companies were fictitious and that he had forged Italian government bonds. His group of companies collapsed and many of them went bankrupt.
277.explanation: Kreuger's dazzling reputation concealed a hollow and fraudulent core that was revealed only when he was gone.
277.tie_back: The kural speaks of people who look as bright red outside as the kundri seed but are black within like its tip, and Kreuger's empire was exactly such a bright surface over a dark centre.
277._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a dazzling exterior hiding a dark interior, though Kreuger's disguise was financial respectability rather than religious piety.

278.event_title: Rasputin gains influence at the Russian court as a holy man
278.event: Grigori Rasputin, a Siberian peasant who presented himself as a wandering holy man, reached St Petersburg in 1903 and from 1905 became close to Tsar Nicholas II and Empress Alexandra, largely because he appeared able to ease the suffering of their son Alexei, who had haemophilia. Reports of his debauched private conduct caused repeated scandal, and in 1911 the prime minister sent the tsar a report on his behaviour. His influence over appointments grew during the First World War until a group of noblemen killed him in December 1916.
278.explanation: Rasputin's reputation for holiness opened the doors of the palace even as reports of his conduct away from it became a national scandal.
278.tie_back: The kural speaks of those with impurity in their minds who live hidden behind an outward show of holiness, a description that fits how Rasputin's critics saw him.
278._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit, though much said about Rasputin in his lifetime was rumour, so the event is limited to the documented scandal and influence.

279.event_title: Joseph Merrick, the Elephant Man, finds a home at the London Hospital
279.event: Joseph Merrick was born with severe physical deformities and was exhibited in a freak show before the surgeon Frederick Treves arranged for him to live at the London Hospital in 1886. Treves at first assumed from his appearance and difficult speech that he was mentally impaired, but came to recognise him as intelligent and sensitive; Merrick could read and write and enjoyed books. Public donations allowed him to remain at the hospital until his death in April 1890 at the age of 27.
279.explanation: Merrick's story is a lasting lesson that a person's appearance can mislead even an expert observer about the person within.
279.tie_back: The kural says the bent-necked lute is sweet while the straight arrow is cruel, so people must be judged by their deeds and not their looks, and Merrick's life taught that lesson to Victorian London.
279._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the lute half of the image, judging by nature not looks, though the kural's main concern is hypocrites who look virtuous.

280.event_title: Erasmus publishes The Praise of Folly
280.place: Western Europe (work of the Dutch humanist Erasmus)
280.event: The Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus published The Praise of Folly, a satire in which Folly herself mocks theologians, monks and rulers, including the monks' pride in their habits, rules and ceremonies. In his earlier Enchiridion of 1503 he had argued that true piety consists not in outward ceremonies but in inward conversion. The satire provoked strong resentment among theologians, and in 1564 it was among his works placed on the Church's index of prohibited books.
280.explanation: Erasmus became the most famous voice of his age for the view that outward religious forms count for nothing without an inward change of life.
280.tie_back: The kural says there is no need to shave the head or grow long hair if one simply gives up what the world condemns, and Erasmus mocked the monks' outward marks while urging inner reform.
280._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the kural's dismissal of ascetic externals in favour of conduct, though it is a literary rather than a dramatic event.
